view: God tested Mecca or Quraysh with drought and famine as He tested the orchard owners by destroying their garden.
note: Several specify seven years, the Prophet's prayer for hardship like Joseph's years against Muḍar, or people reduced to eating carrion, hides, bones, or blood; Ibn ʿĀshūr places the famine after the Hijra. The famine account is distinguished from a trial through prosperity and the Badr interpretation.

view: The Prophet prayed for Muḍar to suffer years of hardship like Joseph's, and Mecca's ensuing famine is invoked to explain its trial in the orchard parable; one account adds disease, death, and lost provisions.
note: The famine account is also used as interpretation, but these notes give the reported prayer and circumstances.

view: The comparison may concern Quraysh at Badr: Abu Jahl ordered captives bound in the mountains rather than killed, and his power over opponents is likened to the owners' power over their orchard.
note: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ describes the Badr version as Quraysh's vow to kill the Prophet and companions followed by defeat; it differs from the captive-binding report.

view: The Badr comparison is rejected as reading later history into the passage: Badr came about five years after this sura, whose warning addresses tyrants generally.
note: Disagreement concerns whether Badr can explain the earlier passage.

view: The deniers' prosperity itself was a trial: wealth, children, security, provision, or trade should have prompted gratitude and obedience, but led to pride, contempt for poor believers, and rejection of the messenger.
note: Rāzī also speaks of a wealthy man; Asad says the owners received affluence beyond their moral deserts. This account locates the test in blessings, whereas the famine account locates it in affliction.

view: The orchard owners were tested through their blessings to thank God and give the poor their due; withholding it brought loss of those blessings.
note: Naḥḥās calls the poor's due obligatory.

view: Divine testing imposes duties so human acts become manifest, although God knew them beforehand; trial, testing, and examination are synonymous, and the expression describes God's treatment of the tested figuratively.
Balāʾ can mean either a trial or the affliction itself; ibtilāʾ means examination.
The plural pronoun refers to the preceding deniers, understood collectively as Quraysh's leaders and, in a broader reading, every contemptible oath breaker.
note: Ibn ʿĀshūr and Iṣlāḥī link the pronoun to the preceding description; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ extends its scope.

view: The kāf marks an accusative modifier of an omitted cognate verbal noun; mā can be a verbal noun or a relative pronoun meaning 'that which.'
The temporal phrase introduced by idh is governed by balawnā.
The owners were a group of heirs, described in some reports as brothers or sons of a formerly charitable father.
note: Accounts differ on number: three heirs or sons in some, five sons in Ibn ʿAbbās's report transmitted by Ṭabāṭabāʾī.

view: Reports place the orchard in Yemen near Ṣanʿāʾ, often at Darwān or a similarly named site; stated distances range from one or two farsakhs to six, nine, or twelve miles.
note: Names given include al-Sarim, Ḍarwān, al-Darawan, Dawran, Ṣarwān, Ṣurawān, Sawran, Dar, and al-Ridwan; Ibn ʿĀshūr says Darwan may name the garden itself. The locations and distances are competing reports.

view: Some reports identify the owners as Abyssinians or Ethiopians whose generous father fed the poor and whose sons called his giving foolish.
note: Their location or identity competes with the Yemenite and Israelite accounts.

view: Other reports identify the owners or their father as People of the Book or Israelites; one says the father was a righteous believer without specifying Jewish or Christian identity.
note: This identity differs from the Abyssinian, Thaqīf, and unbeliever accounts.

view: A reported Jewish identification is argued from Yemen's Jewish past and a Torah requirement to tithe fruit.
note: Ibn ʿĀshūr notes that the account attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās does not specify Jewish or Christian identity.

view: Some accounts place the owners shortly after Jesus, including an account of Muslims after Jesus and one of people near Ṣanʿāʾ before Christianity spread in Yemen.
note: Ibn ʿĀshūr dates Christianity's spread there to the Abyssinian conquest near the Year of the Elephant.

view: One report calls the owners unbelievers, whereas a majority account says they were otherwise; the blight destroyed their orchard.
note: The dispute concerns the owners' religious identity.

view: Accounts associate the estate with Thaqīf in Yemen and describe its former owner as a Muslim who gave the poor a share at harvest.
note: The attribution differs from Abyssinian and Israelite identifications.

view: The former owner kept enough food for his household, sometimes a year's provision, and gave the remaining harvest to the poor.
note: Ṭabāṭabāʾī's report says the father gave each rightful person a share.

view: The former owner let poor people collect missed or fallen dates, grapes, grain, and other gleanings after harvest; reports mention windfall fruit and sizable crops gathered beneath palms.
note: Al-Farrāʾ names poor people, widows, and orphans; one account says the father took the poor with him to harvest, while another says he alerted them.

view: After their father's death, the heirs feared that many dependents and diminished resources made his charity unaffordable; they resolved to harvest secretly before the poor arrived and deny them their customary share.
note: Some heirs called their father's generosity foolish; some accounts say they feared poverty rather than reporting actual diminished wealth. The early harvest avoided notifying the poor.

view: A hesitant brother opposed the plan, warned the others to fear God and remember His punishment, and was overruled; an oath may have secured his participation.
note: One report counts five sons, four agreeing and the moderate brother objecting.

view: Their confident oath presumed the orchard safe from calamity because it had survived changing weather.
Beginning the social parable with an oath presents a communal enterprise founded on agreement; that oath governs its later profit or loss.
The owners' oath echoes the earlier mention of a frequent swearer and warns that firm vows made without considering one's knowledge or power can bring disaster.
Their resolve to deny the poor was blameworthy before they acted; actually taking property and denying rights would be worse.
Because no one can be sure a future statement will come true, the owners' blame for omitting an exception supports requiring one when speaking about the future.
note: The omission is debated as failing to say 'if God wills' or failing to reserve the poor's share.

view: Ṣarm denotes cutting, especially picking dates or other fruit and harvesting crops; related terms include ṣarām and jadhādh for harvest, and aṣrama for palms ready to harvest.
note: The root also denotes complete severance and separation between companions; a line of Imruʾ al-Qays illustrates severing a relationship.

view: A line by Imruʾ al-Qays uses ṣaram for cutting off or severing a relationship, illustrating the verb's root meaning beyond harvest.
Saying they would cut the garden, rather than merely gather fruit, conveys complete severance; their words came true through its ruin, against their intention and without their own hands causing it.
note: Al-Biqāʿī stresses how complete removal would keep the poor from sharing.

view: They swore to cut and gather the orchard's fruit early the next morning, before poor people learned of the harvest.
note: Several say they would work in late-night or predawn darkness, called sadfa by al-Wāḥidī.

view: Muṣbiḥīn means entering the morning; accounts describe the planned harvest at dawn, often while it was still dark.
note: Al-Samīn compares 37:137 and a proverb about a traveler arrived by morning.

view: Muṣbiḥīn is a circumstantial expression describing the subject of 'they will cut it.'
Layaṣrimunnahā answers the oath and reports their words in the third person; direct quotation of their own oath would use 'we will cut it.'
One explanation of making no exception is that they did not say 'if God wills' in their oath, trusting too confidently that they could harvest.
note: Al-Kashshāf calls the phrase a condition functioning as an exception because the meanings coincide; this competes with the explanation that they reserved no share for the poor.

view: Another explanation of making no exception is that they meant to leave none of the harvest for the poor.
note: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ prefers this plain story and rejects reducing the matter to omission of 'if God wills.'

view: Janna here means a worldly garden or orchard; its root evokes concealment and is also reflected in words for embryo, jinn, insanity, night, and shield.
note: Elmalılı also suggests an earthly paradise and, at a deeper level, a homeland.

view: Although janna became the Islamic name for Paradise and is often used that way in the Qur'an, context can identify an earthly garden; the Qur'an uses that sense in nine singular, five dual, and twelve plural verses.
The definite article can be generic in a parable, presenting a complete situation without identifying a particular historical orchard or Yemenite owners.
note: This contrasts with reports locating an actual orchard near Ṣanʿāʾ.

view: Calling them plural owners suggests common property and a social or national parable, unlike the single owner's garden in al-Kahf.
The garden is reported to have contained palms, crops, and grapes and to have passed to its owners from their fathers.
The orchard was destroyed or burned overnight after the heirs planned to deprive the poor; descriptions include ashes and a blackened, uprooted garden.
note: Accounts vary on the manner of destruction.

view: One report says Gabriel swept up the garden, carried it around the Kaaba, and placed it where Ṭāʾif stands, accounting for the town's name and fertility.
note: Al-Bakrī gives a competing account of the town's name.

view: Al-Bakrī derives Ṭāʾif's name from a man of Ṣadaf who built a wall around the town.
note: This differs from the report that Gabriel moved the orchard there.

view: One account says God replaced the owners' garden with a better one, after which they again planned to harvest secretly before dawn without saying 'if God wills.'
note: This sequence differs from accounts placing the secret oath before the garden's destruction.

view: Reports say the owners repented and received a better garden; one says their sincerity brought a replacement called al-Ḥayawān, with grape clusters so large a donkey was needed to carry one.
When asked whether the garden owners belonged to Paradise or Hell, Qatāda said the question burdened him.
Harvesters should share crops with poor people present, beyond zakat; the view preferred by al-Qurṭubī prohibits harvesting at night to evade this right, citing 6:141.
The calamity that came upon the orchard was a destructive trial, described as a night visitor or punishment arriving at night.
The word for the calamity has the variant reading ṭayf alongside ṭāʾif.
Al-ṣarīm can describe the garden as cut down, black as night, dried like daytime vegetation, empty, or sandy; ṣārimīn means harvesters.
note: These are alternative senses of a later word in the orchard episode.

view: The phrase 'go to your field' uses ʿalā because they went to cut and harvest it; alternatively 'went' means 'turned toward,' as in going against an enemy.
Yatakhāfatūn means whispering; khafiya, khafata, and khafada all denote concealment, and al-khafdūd names a bat.
The later phrase 'that no poor person enter' is explanatory; Ibn Masʿūd's reading omits 'that' and supplies 'they say'; the ban means denying entry.
Ḥard can describe a year withholding its good, camels withholding milk, or the sons' resolve and speed to deprive the poor.
note: A poem and the name of swift birds support the speed sense; their attempt to deprive the poor left them deprived instead.

view: An alternative takes ḥard as the anger the owners could muster toward one another, in line with their subsequent mutual blame.
note: This differs from senses of resolve, speed, or withholding.

view: Ḥard may be the proper name of the orchard.
note: This differs from treating the word as a quality of their action.

view: The phrase involving ḥard may mean the sons assumed their planned harvest and deprivation would succeed.
At first the ruined garden looked so unfamiliar that the owners thought they had lost their way; recognizing it, they admitted that their wrongdoing had deprived them.
Awsaṭuhum means the most just and best among them, from language for a person in the middle of their people; compare the 'middle community.'
The moderate brother's call to glorify God most likely urged remembrance and repentance from the corrupt plan before punishment; the others heeded him too late.
note: This competes with explanations of glorifying as saying 'if God wills' or praying.

view: An alternative takes the call to glorify God as urging the oath's exception, 'if God wills,' since entrusting the matter to God magnifies Him.
Al-Ḥasan interprets the call to glorify God as prayer; neglecting prayer explains why it did not restrain the plan or prompt an exception.
By saying 'Glory be to our Lord,' the owners denied injustice in God and confessed their own wrong in withholding charity and omitting an exception.
They blamed one another because some proposed the plan, some accepted it, some opposed it, and some silently approved.
The verb yabdilanā has readings with and without doubling.
Their declaration that they were rāghibūn to their Lord means seeking good from Him and hoping for pardon.
Their worldly punishment resembles that of Mecca's people, while punishment in the afterlife is greater.
Quraysh's test through Muhammad and his guidance parallels the brothers' test through their father's practice and religious obligations.
As the orchard owners were punished in this life, Quraysh faced worldly punishment, and repentance remained open to survivors as it did to the brothers.
The parable invites Meccan unbelievers to reflect and return to God.
The story warns deniers that blessings and power can vanish suddenly, leaving loss, useless grief, and repentance too late.
note: Iṣlāḥī applies the reversal specifically to Quraysh leaders' authority; Kur'an Yolu adds loss of prosperity and trade and eventual defeat.

view: The orchard parable follows a portrait of wealth and children and warns that pride in provision leads to contempt for truth and ingratitude; comparable stories include the garden in al-Kahf and Qārūn.
note: Ibn ʿĀshūr says the parable opens a new section.

view: The story illustrates a recurring divine law across generations, rather than an isolated event in Muhammad's time.
If these verses were revealed with the preceding passage, the warning applies to deniers generally and recalls their surprising defeat at Badr as worldly proof that apparent causes can fail.
note: This is a conditional allusion to Badr, distinct from making Badr the occasion of revelation.

view: The sura's overall context is Meccan, but the seventeen verses about the garden owners may have been revealed in Medina.
The sura is early Meccan except verses 17–33 and 48–50; it is commonly placed second after al-ʿAlaq, though its ordering is disputed and it reflects the first revelation's atmosphere.
The sura consoles the Prophet after accusations of madness, promises reward, praises his character, forbids compromise with opponents, and commands patience for God's judgment.
A reported interpretation places the previously threatened mark on the arrogant man's nose on Judgment Day as humiliation for his pride.
note: This note concerns preceding context supplied with the verse's sources.

view: Qatāda says the orchard owners are people whose story God has recounted and made clear.
